Lab 5: Latent Variables: Factor Models, IRT, and Measurement Invariance

Intermediate Quantitative Methods · Week 5

Author

Sebastian Ramirez-Ruiz

Term

Autumn 2026

Welcome! 👋

Last week we built a scale by averaging items. This week’s seminar replaced the average with a model: a latent variable that causes the answers, plus noise. Today we fit those models in R. The lab has three parts, plus an optional fourth:

  • First, we run an exploratory factor analysis (EFA) on the trust battery: how many factors, and which items go where?
  • Second, we write the two competing theories as confirmatory factor analyses (CFA), compare them, and compute McDonald’s ω by hand.
  • Third, we fit item response theory (IRT) models to a political knowledge quiz and read their information curves.
  • Fourth, optional and on your own: we test whether the trust measure travels across countries (measurement invariance). Martín will not cover this part in the lab.

Along the way, we practice the R skills from Lab 4 (writing and testing functions, iterating with {purrr}, reshaping with {tidyr}) and add two new ones: building grids with tidyr::expand_grid() and running a function once per row of a table with purrr::pmap().

As last week, every data set is simulated, so we know the truth and can check whether the models recover it.

Plan for today ≈ time
Exploratory factor analysis: how many factors, and which items go where 30 min
Confirmatory factor analysis: one form of trust or two? McDonald’s ω 35 min
Item response theory: a knowledge quiz and its information curve 45 min
Wrap-up 10 min
Optional, on your own: does the trust measure travel? (invariance) —

Packages 📦

# Install these in your CONSOLE if you have not done so yet:
# install.packages(c("tidyverse", "psych", "GPArotation", "lavaan", "mirt", "remotes"))
# {ggmirt} is not on CRAN; install it from GitHub:
# remotes::install_github("masurp/ggmirt")

library(tidyverse) # data wrangling and plots; loads {dplyr}, {tidyr}, {purrr}, {ggplot2}
library(psych) # exploratory factor analysis
library(GPArotation) # rotations used by psych::fa()
library(lavaan) # confirmatory factor analysis
library(mirt) # item response theory
library(ggmirt) # ready-made ggplot2 plots for {mirt} models

We call MASS::mvrnorm() once, to draw correlated latent variables. {MASS} ships with R, so there is nothing to install, and we do not load it: library(MASS) would mask dplyr::select().

Part I: Exploratory factor analysis 🔍

Our data: the trust battery again 🏛

We return to the battery from Lab 4, now with eight items. In the seminar we asked whether political trust is one attitude or two: trust in the representative institutions that win elections, and trust in the order institutions that implement and enforce the law. Our simulated world has two correlated factors (r = 0.6):

Item Factor Question (0 = no trust at all, 10 = complete trust)
parliament representative How much do you trust the national parliament?
politicians representative How much do you trust politicians?
parties representative How much do you trust political parties?
government representative How much do you trust the national government?
dont_care_r representative “Politicians don’t care what people like me think” (reverse-coded)
courts order How much do you trust the legal system?
police order How much do you trust the police?
civil_service order How much do you trust the civil service?

We write the data-generating process as a function of the sample size, so that we can draw new samples whenever we need them. It also takes two latent means and a shift in the police item, which only the optional Part IV uses; the defaults switch them off.

make_trust <- function(n, mean_rep = 0, mean_ord = 0, police_shift = 0) {
  # two latent factors, correlated 0.6, with variance 1
  latent <- MASS::mvrnorm(n, mu = c(mean_rep, mean_ord),
                          Sigma = matrix(c(1, 0.6, 0.6, 1), nrow = 2))

  # loadings: how strongly each item reflects each factor
  loadings <- rbind(
    parliament    = c(0.85, 0),
    politicians   = c(0.80, 0),
    parties       = c(0.75, 0),
    government    = c(0.75, 0),
    dont_care_r   = c(0.50, 0),
    courts        = c(0, 0.80),
    police        = c(0, 0.70),
    civil_service = c(0, 0.60)
  )

  # each item = loading x factor + noise, so that every item has variance 1
  noise_sd <- sqrt(1 - rowSums(loadings^2))
  raw <- latent %*% t(loadings) +
    matrix(rnorm(n * 8), nrow = n) %*% diag(noise_sd)
  colnames(raw) <- rownames(loadings)

  # Part IV: people answer the police item more positively than their trust predicts
  raw[, "police"] <- raw[, "police"] + police_shift

  tibble::as_tibble(raw) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(parliament:civil_service,
                                \(x) pmin(pmax(round(5 + 2 * x), 0), 10)))
}

Two pieces of matrix algebra do the work. latent %*% t(loadings) multiplies each respondent’s two factor scores by each item’s two loadings and adds them up, giving an n × 8 matrix. The noise term draws n × 8 standard normal values and scales each column by its own standard deviation. The last line turns each item into a 0–10 answer, as in Lab 4.

trust <- make_trust(n = 1500)
items <- dplyr::select(trust, parliament:civil_service)

head(trust)

Step 1: Is there anything to factor? 🔗

Factor analysis models the correlations between items. If they were all close to zero, there would be nothing to explain. A heat map, as in Lab 4:

cor(items) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column("item_1") %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-item_1, names_to = "item_2", values_to = "r") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(c(item_1, item_2), \(x) factor(x, levels = names(items)))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = item_1, y = item_2, fill = r)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(r, 2)), size = 3.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#cc0065", mid = "white", high = "#2f1a61", limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Correlation")

Turning the item names into a factor() with levels = names(items) keeps the questionnaire order on both axes; otherwise ggplot sorts them alphabetically and the two blocks disappear.

Step 2: How many factors? Eigenvalues and parallel analysis 📉

In the seminar, the eigenvalues of the correlation matrix told us how much of the total variance each successive dimension captures. Eight items have eight eigenvalues, which add up to 8:

ev_observed <- eigen(cor(items))$values
round(ev_observed, 2)
[1] 3.81 1.23 0.72 0.58 0.48 0.44 0.41 0.33

How large is “large”? Parallel analysis compares each eigenvalue with what we would get from random data of the same size: eight unrelated items and 1,500 respondents. Keep the factors whose eigenvalues beat chance.

We can write it ourselves. One function simulates a random data set and returns its eigenvalues; purrr::map() repeats it 100 times:

random_eigenvalues <- function(n, k) {
  noise <- matrix(rnorm(n * k), nrow = n)
  eigen(cor(noise))$values
}

ev_random <- purrr::map(1:100, \(i) random_eigenvalues(n = nrow(items), k = ncol(items))) %>%
  purrr::reduce(`+`) / 100 # average over the 100 draws

round(ev_random, 2)
[1] 1.11 1.07 1.04 1.01 0.99 0.96 0.93 0.89

purrr::reduce(+) adds the 100 vectors together, element by element; dividing by 100 gives the average random eigenvalue for each position.

tibble::tibble(dimension = 1:8, Observed = ev_observed, `Random data` = ev_random) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-dimension, names_to = "data", values_to = "eigenvalue") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = dimension, y = eigenvalue, color = data)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:8) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Observed" = "#2f1a61", "Random data" = "#cc0065")) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Dimension", y = "Eigenvalue", color = NULL)

psych::fa.parallel() does the same thing (with eigenvalues from a factor model rather than from the raw correlations) and prints its suggestion:

pa <- psych::fa.parallel(items, fa = "fa", plot = FALSE)
Parallel analysis suggests that the number of factors =  2  and the number of components =  NA

Activity 💡

  1. How many eigenvalues are larger than 1 (the old “Kaiser rule”)? How many beat the random eigenvalues? Do the two rules agree here?
  2. Simulate a data set with one factor only: copy make_trust(), set both columns of the loadings matrix to load on the first factor (move the order loadings to the first column), and rerun the parallel analysis. What does it suggest now?
➨ Click for Answer 🔓 
# 1.
sum(ev_observed > 1)
[1] 2
sum(ev_observed > ev_random)
[1] 2
# 2. a one-factor world: every item loads on the first factor
latent_1 <- rnorm(1500)
lambda_1 <- c(0.85, 0.80, 0.75, 0.75, 0.50, 0.80, 0.70, 0.60)
one_factor_items <- purrr::map(lambda_1, \(l) l * latent_1 + rnorm(1500, 0, sqrt(1 - l^2))) %>%
  setNames(names(items)) %>%
  tibble::as_tibble() %>%
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(everything(), \(x) pmin(pmax(round(5 + 2 * x), 0), 10)))

pa_one <- psych::fa.parallel(one_factor_items, fa = "fa", plot = FALSE)
Parallel analysis suggests that the number of factors =  1  and the number of components =  NA
  1. Two eigenvalues are larger than 1, and the same two beat the random data: here the rules agree. They often don’t. With 1,500 respondents, random eigenvalues sit close to 1, so the two rules are nearly the same test. With a few hundred respondents and many items, the first random eigenvalues are well above 1, and the Kaiser rule keeps factors that are pure noise. Parallel analysis adapts to the size of the data, which is why it is the better default.
  2. With a single factor in the data-generating process, parallel analysis suggests one factor. (Writing the simulation by hand is a shortcut: a few lines are enough to draw the items.)

Steps 3 and 4: Extract, rotate, and name the factors 🧭

psych::fa() estimates the factor model. We ask for two factors, estimated by maximum likelihood (fm = "ml"), with an oblique rotation (rotate = "oblimin"), which lets the factors correlate:

efa_2 <- psych::fa(items, nfactors = 2, fm = "ml", rotate = "oblimin")

print(efa_2$loadings, cutoff = 0.3)

Loadings:
              ML1    ML2   
parliament     0.858       
politicians    0.756       
parties        0.714       
government     0.731       
dont_care_r    0.503       
courts                0.774
police                0.704
civil_service         0.617

                 ML1   ML2
SS loadings    2.605 1.479
Proportion Var 0.326 0.185
Cumulative Var 0.326 0.511

cutoff = 0.3 hides small loadings so that the pattern is easier to see. The factor correlation is stored in Phi:

round(efa_2$Phi, 2)
    ML1 ML2
ML1 1.0 0.6
ML2 0.6 1.0

The two factors are clearly separate (each item loads on one of them) and clearly related (r ≈ 0.6). Naming them is our job, not the computer’s: the first looks like representative trust, the second like order trust.

A loading matrix is easier to read as a plot. We turn it into a tibble and pivot it longer, exactly as we did with the correlation matrix:

loadings_tidy <- function(efa) {
  unclass(efa$loadings) %>%
    as.data.frame() %>%
    tibble::rownames_to_column("item") %>%
    tidyr::pivot_longer(-item, names_to = "factor", values_to = "loading") %>%
    dplyr::mutate(item = factor(item, levels = rev(names(items))))
}

ggplot(loadings_tidy(efa_2), aes(x = factor, y = item, fill = loading)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(loading, 2)), size = 3.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#cc0065", mid = "white", high = "#2f1a61", limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Loading")

unclass() strips the special loadings class, which otherwise prints in its own format, and leaves a plain matrix.

Activity 💡

  1. Refit the model with an orthogonal rotation (rotate = "varimax"), which forces the factors to be uncorrelated. Plot the loadings with loadings_tidy(). What happens to the small loadings, and why?
  2. Fit three factors (with oblimin). What does the third factor look like? Would you be able to name it?
➨ Click for Answer 🔓 
efa_varimax <- psych::fa(items, nfactors = 2, fm = "ml", rotate = "varimax")
efa_3 <- psych::fa(items, nfactors = 3, fm = "ml", rotate = "oblimin")

dplyr::bind_rows(
  loadings_tidy(efa_varimax) %>% dplyr::mutate(model = "2 factors, varimax"),
  loadings_tidy(efa_3) %>% dplyr::mutate(model = "3 factors, oblimin")
) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = factor, y = item, fill = loading)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(loading, 2)), size = 3.2) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#cc0065", mid = "white", high = "#2f1a61", limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  facet_wrap(~ model, scales = "free_x") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Loading")
  1. With varimax, every item picks up a cross-loading on the other factor. The factors really are correlated, and if the rotation forbids them to correlate, that shared variance has to go somewhere: into the loadings. The structure is blurrier, for no substantive gain. This is why oblique rotation is the sensible default for political attitudes.
  2. The third factor is essentially one item: parties moves over to it (with a small loading from dont_care_r), splitting the representative block. A factor that one item defines is not a construct, and there is no substantive name for it: in our simulated world, it is noise. Parallel analysis said two; a factor you cannot interpret is a sign of over-extraction. In real data, look at the wording of the items before you decide (is there something about parties that the other items lack?).

Part II: Confirmatory factor analysis 🧩

Two theories, written down 📝

The EFA let the data choose the structure. In a CFA, we choose it: we say which item loads on which factor, and every other loading is fixed at zero. Then we ask whether the data are consistent with that structure.

{lavaan} uses a model syntax in which =~ reads “is measured by”. The two theories from the seminar:

model_one <- "
  trust =~ parliament + politicians + parties + government + dont_care_r +
           courts + police + civil_service
"

model_two <- "
  representative =~ parliament + politicians + parties + government + dont_care_r
  order          =~ courts + police + civil_service
"

cfa_one <- lavaan::cfa(model_one, data = trust)
cfa_two <- lavaan::cfa(model_two, data = trust)

By default lavaan fixes the first loading of each factor to 1 (the marker item), which gives the factor the scale of that item, and lets the two factors correlate.

Comparing the two theories ⚖️

From the seminar: the χ² test asks whether the model-implied covariance matrix \(\hat\Sigma = \Lambda\Phi\Lambda' + \Theta\) is exactly right (it almost never is in large samples), so we also read approximate fit indices. We write a small function that collects the ones we need into a one-row tibble, and apply it to both models:

fit_table <- function(fit) {
  lavaan::fitMeasures(fit, c("chisq", "df", "cfi", "tli", "rmsea", "srmr")) %>%
    as.list() %>%
    tibble::as_tibble() %>%
    dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(everything(), \(x) round(x, 3)))
}

list("One factor" = cfa_one, "Two factors" = cfa_two) %>%
  purrr::map(fit_table) %>%
  purrr::list_rbind(names_to = "model")

The usual rules of thumb are CFI ≥ 0.95, RMSEA ≤ 0.06, and SRMR ≤ 0.08. The one-factor model fails the first two clearly and sits right at the SRMR cutoff, a reminder that the indices do not always agree. The two-factor model passes all three comfortably. The models are nested (one factor is two factors whose correlation is fixed to 1), so we can also test the difference directly:

lavaan::lavTestLRT(cfa_one, cfa_two)

Where does one factor fail? Residual correlations 🌡

A fit index tells us that a model fails, not where. The residual correlations, observed minus model-implied, tell us where:

residual_heatmap <- function(fit) {
  lavaan::lavResiduals(fit, type = "cor")$cov %>%
    as.data.frame() %>%
    tibble::rownames_to_column("item_1") %>%
    tidyr::pivot_longer(-item_1, names_to = "item_2", values_to = "residual") %>%
    dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(c(item_1, item_2), \(x) factor(x, levels = names(items)))) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = item_1, y = item_2, fill = residual)) +
    geom_tile(color = "white") +
    geom_text(aes(label = round(residual, 2)), size = 3.2) +
    scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#cc0065", mid = "white", high = "#2f1a61", limits = c(-0.4, 0.4)) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Residual\ncorrelation")
}

residual_heatmap(cfa_one)

Activity 💡

  1. Describe the pattern of residuals for the one-factor model. Which items does the model fail to explain, and in which direction?
  2. Run residual_heatmap(cfa_two). What changed?
➨ Click for Answer 🔓 
residual_heatmap(cfa_two)
  1. The order items (courts, police, civil_service) are more correlated with each other than one factor can explain (positive residuals of about 0.25 in the bottom-right block). Correlations between the two blocks are over-predicted (small negative residuals). The representative items are reproduced well: there are five of them, so they dominate the single factor, and the order items are left over. One factor cannot be two things at once.
  2. With two factors, all residuals are close to zero: the model reproduces the correlation matrix. This is the logic of the seminar’s “where does one form fail” slide.

McDonald’s ω by hand ✍️

Lab 4 ended with a promise: α assumes that all items measure the construct equally well, and our items don’t. McDonald’s ω uses the fitted loadings instead. With standardized loadings \(\lambda_j\) and residual variances \(\theta_j = 1 - \lambda_j^2\):

\[\omega = \frac{\left(\sum_j \lambda_j\right)^2}{\left(\sum_j \lambda_j\right)^2 + \sum_j \theta_j}\]

The numerator is the variance of the sum score that comes from the factor; the denominator is the total variance of the sum score. ω is computed one factor at a time. lavaan::standardizedSolution() returns all the standardized estimates in one table; we need the loadings (op == "=~") of one factor and the residual variances (op == "~~", an item with itself) of its items:

omega_by_hand <- function(fit, factor_name) {
  est <- lavaan::standardizedSolution(fit)

  lambda <- est %>%
    dplyr::filter(op == "=~", lhs == factor_name) %>%
    dplyr::pull(est.std)

  item_names <- est %>%
    dplyr::filter(op == "=~", lhs == factor_name) %>%
    dplyr::pull(rhs)

  theta <- est %>%
    dplyr::filter(op == "~~", lhs %in% item_names, lhs == rhs) %>%
    dplyr::pull(est.std)

  sum(lambda)^2 / (sum(lambda)^2 + sum(theta))
}

omega_by_hand(cfa_two, "representative")
[1] 0.8414896
omega_by_hand(cfa_two, "order")
[1] 0.74135

We bring back Lab 4’s α function to compare, on the same items:

cronbach_alpha <- function(items) {
  k <- ncol(items)
  item_variances <- purrr::map_dbl(items, var)
  total_variance <- var(rowSums(items))
  (k / (k - 1)) * (1 - sum(item_variances) / total_variance)
}

tibble::tibble(
  factor = c("representative", "order"),
  alpha = c(cronbach_alpha(dplyr::select(trust, parliament:dont_care_r)),
            cronbach_alpha(dplyr::select(trust, courts:civil_service))),
  omega = c(omega_by_hand(cfa_two, "representative"),
            omega_by_hand(cfa_two, "order"))
) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(c(alpha, omega), \(x) round(x, 3)))

ω is only slightly higher than α. α is a lower bound that is reached when all loadings are equal; our loadings differ (0.85 down to 0.50 for the representative items), but not by enough to open a large gap. With very unequal loadings, or items that also load on a second factor, the two coefficients can differ much more.

⚠️ ω is only as good as the model it comes from. You can compute ω for all eight items from cfa_one, and it will look respectable, but the model behind it fits badly: it is the reliability of a sum score for a construct that the data say is not one thing. Check the structure first, then report reliability per factor. (semTools::compRelSEM() computes ω for every factor of a lavaan model, if you want to check your function against a package.)

Part III: Item response theory 🎓

A political knowledge quiz 🗳

Factor models treat answers as continuous. Many measures are right or wrong: political knowledge quizzes, literacy tests, the INSPIRE items from the seminar. IRT models the probability of a correct answer as a function of the latent ability \(\theta\).

We simulate a 12-item political knowledge quiz, answered by 1,500 people. Each question has four options, so someone who knows nothing gets it right 25% of the time by guessing. The three-parameter logistic model (3PL) from the seminar:

\[P(\text{correct}_{ij}) = g_j + (1 - g_j)\,\frac{1}{1 + \exp\{-a_j(\theta_i - b_j)\}}\]

with discrimination \(a_j\), difficulty \(b_j\), and guessing \(g_j\). We store the item parameters in a table, one row per item:

quiz_items <- tibble::tibble(
  item = sprintf("q%02d", 1:12), # q01, q02, ..., q12
  a = c(1.6, 1.2, 2.0, 0.9, 1.4, 1.8, 0.5, 1.3, 1.7, 1.1, 2.2, 1.0),
  b = c(-2.0, -1.5, -1.0, -0.6, -0.3, 0, 0.2, 0.5, 0.8, 1.1, 1.5, 2.0),
  g = 0.25
)

quiz_items

sprintf("q%02d", 1:12) pads the numbers with a leading zero, so that the items sort correctly.

The probability itself is a one-line function. Then purrr::pmap() calls a function once per row of a table, matching the columns to the arguments by name. Each call draws 1,500 answers (1 = correct) for one item:

p_correct <- function(theta, a, b, g) {
  g + (1 - g) * plogis(a * (theta - b))
}

n <- 1500
knowledge <- rnorm(n) # latent political knowledge (unobservable!)

quiz <- purrr::pmap(quiz_items, \(item, a, b, g) {
  rbinom(n, size = 1, prob = p_correct(knowledge, a, b, g))
}) %>%
  setNames(quiz_items$item) %>%
  tibble::as_tibble()

head(quiz)
colMeans(quiz) %>% round(2) # share answering each item correctly
 q01  q02  q03  q04  q05  q06  q07  q08  q09  q10  q11  q12 
0.94 0.85 0.83 0.70 0.66 0.62 0.60 0.53 0.45 0.43 0.35 0.37

plogis() is the logistic function \(1 / (1 + e^{-x})\), so p_correct() is the 3PL formula written in R.

Rasch, 2PL, or 3PL? ⚖️

mirt::mirt() fits all three. The 1 says the model has one latent dimension:

irt_rasch <- mirt::mirt(quiz, 1, itemtype = "Rasch", verbose = FALSE)
irt_2pl <- mirt::mirt(quiz, 1, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE)
irt_3pl <- mirt::mirt(quiz, 1, itemtype = "3PL", verbose = FALSE,
                      technical = list(NCYCLES = 2000))

The 3PL is hard to estimate, so we give the algorithm more iterations than the default 500 (NCYCLES). The models are nested (Rasch ⊂ 2PL ⊂ 3PL), and anova() compares them:

anova(irt_rasch, irt_2pl)
anova(irt_2pl, irt_3pl)

The 2PL clearly beats the Rasch model: the items differ in how well they discriminate. The 3PL improves the likelihood and the AIC, but the BIC, which penalizes the twelve extra parameters more heavily, prefers the 2PL. And mirt warns that even after 2,000 iterations the 3PL has not converged. We know the data come from a 3PL, so this is worth a moment. Look at its estimates, in the usual \(a\), \(b\), \(g\) form (IRTpars = TRUE):

coef(irt_3pl, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items %>%
  round(2)
       a     b    g u
q01 2.13 -0.93 0.76 1
q02 0.94 -1.98 0.10 1
q03 1.94 -1.21 0.05 1
q04 0.75 -0.86 0.17 1
q05 0.99 -0.78 0.01 1
q06 2.22  0.14 0.30 1
q07 1.14  1.27 0.47 1
q08 1.41  0.63 0.29 1
q09 1.48  0.84 0.23 1
q10 1.25  1.15 0.24 1
q11 1.57  1.58 0.24 1
q12 0.79  1.78 0.20 1

All guessing parameters are truly 0.25. The estimates scatter widely, and several difficulties and discriminations are far off with them. Compare q01: truly a very easy item (\(b = -2\)), estimated as a medium item that people often guess right. Over the range where most respondents are, the two descriptions give nearly the same curve, so the data cannot tell them apart. To pin down \(g_j\), we need many people with very low knowledge answering item \(j\), and for the easy items there are hardly any.

The usual fix comes from the design of the test, not from the data: with four options, a blind guess is right a quarter of the time. We fix every \(g_j\) at 0.25 and estimate only \(a\) and \(b\). In mirt, a model with constraints is written with mirt.model(): START sets the starting value of a parameter, and FIXED keeps it there.

model_fixed_g <- mirt::mirt.model("
  knowledge = 1-12
  START = (1-12, g, 0.25)
  FIXED = (1-12, g)
")

irt_fixed_g <- mirt::mirt(quiz, model_fixed_g, itemtype = "3PL", verbose = FALSE)

coef(irt_fixed_g, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items %>%
  round(2)
       a     b    g u
q01 1.35 -2.35 0.25 1
q02 1.01 -1.64 0.25 1
q03 2.30 -0.92 0.25 1
q04 0.82 -0.57 0.25 1
q05 1.29 -0.19 0.25 1
q06 1.86  0.04 0.25 1
q07 0.52  0.31 0.25 1
q08 1.25  0.54 0.25 1
q09 1.59  0.88 0.25 1
q10 1.30  1.17 0.25 1
q11 1.71  1.59 0.25 1
q12 1.10  1.78 0.25 1

Now the estimates are close to the truth. This model has as many free parameters as the 2PL (12 discriminations, 12 difficulties), so we can compare the two directly on AIC and BIC:

anova(irt_2pl, irt_fixed_g)

The 3PL with fixed guessing wins on both criteria. (anova() prints no test here, because the models are not nested: neither is a special case of the other.)

Activity 💡

Print the 2PL estimates with coef(irt_2pl, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items and compare them with the truth in quiz_items. Which items does the 2PL get most wrong, and in which direction? Why would ignoring guessing do that?

➨ Click for Answer 🔓 
coef(irt_2pl, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items %>%
  round(2)
       a     b g u
q01 1.22 -2.78 0 1
q02 0.90 -2.21 0 1
q03 1.74 -1.32 0 1
q04 0.70 -1.34 0 1
q05 1.02 -0.79 0 1
q06 1.19 -0.52 0 1
q07 0.38 -1.07 0 1
q08 0.76 -0.19 0 1
q09 0.78  0.26 0 1
q10 0.61  0.50 0 1
q11 0.50  1.32 0 1
q12 0.45  1.19 0 1

The 2PL gets the hard items most wrong: it makes them look easier (lower \(b\)) and much less discriminating (lower \(a\)) than they are. Without a guessing floor, the 2PL has to explain why a quarter of the people with low knowledge answer a hard item correctly, and the only way it can is to flatten the curve. For easy items, almost everyone answers correctly anyway, so guessing matters less. The model choice is not only about fit statistics: knowing how the test was built (four options) told us which model to use.

Item characteristic curves 📈

{ggmirt} draws the standard IRT plots straight from a fitted mirt model. Each function returns an ordinary ggplot object, so we change its look with the usual + syntax:

ggmirt::tracePlot(irt_fixed_g, facet = FALSE, legend = TRUE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.25, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  scale_color_hue(breaks = paste("item", 1:12), labels = names(quiz)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = NULL, x = "Political knowledge (θ)", y = "P(correct answer)", color = NULL)

{ggmirt} calls the items “item 1” to “item 12” and sorts them as text (1, 10, 11, 12, 2, …). The breaks and labels of the color scale put them back in order, with our names. Adding a new color scale replaces the package’s default, which is why the colors change too.

No curve goes below 0.25, the guessing floor (dashed). Each curve is steepest at its difficulty \(b_j\), and how steep it is there depends on \(a_j\). Items with high discrimination separate people just below their difficulty from people just above it.

Information: where is the test precise? 🔦

The seminar’s key IRT idea: a test is not equally precise everywhere. For a 2PL item, the information at \(\theta\) is

\[I_j(\theta) = a_j^2 \, P_j(\theta)\,\bigl(1 - P_j(\theta)\bigr)\]

It peaks at \(\theta = b_j\), and it is higher for more discriminating items. With guessing, a correct answer is weaker evidence, because it might be a lucky guess, and the formula picks up a penalty:

\[I_j(\theta) = a_j^2 \, \frac{1 - P_j(\theta)}{P_j(\theta)} \left(\frac{P_j(\theta) - g_j}{1 - g_j}\right)^2\]

With \(g_j = 0\) the two formulas are identical. The test information is the sum over items, and the standard error of a person’s score is \(1 / \sqrt{I(\theta)}\).

{ggmirt} will plot all of this for us. But we also want to see what the plots are made of, and we need the numbers for the activity below. So we compute the information ourselves. tidyr::expand_grid() builds every combination of its inputs: here, every item with every value of \(\theta\) on a grid. Then we apply p_correct() and the formula, and sum by \(\theta\):

pars_3pl <- coef(irt_fixed_g, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column("item") %>%
  dplyr::select(item, a, b, g)

icc <- tidyr::expand_grid(pars_3pl, theta = seq(-4, 4, by = 0.05)) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(p = p_correct(theta, a, b, g),
                info = a^2 * ((1 - p) / p) * ((p - g) / (1 - g))^2)

test_info <- icc %>%
  dplyr::group_by(theta) %>%
  dplyr::summarize(info = sum(info)) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(se = 1 / sqrt(info))

As in Lab 4, we check our function against a known answer. mirt::testinfo() computes the same quantity from the fitted model:

mirt_info <- mirt::testinfo(irt_fixed_g, Theta = matrix(test_info$theta))
max(abs(mirt_info - test_info$info)) # should be (almost) zero
[1] 3.552714e-15

Now the plots. Item information first, one curve per item:

ggmirt::itemInfoPlot(irt_fixed_g, facet = FALSE, legend = TRUE) +
  scale_color_hue(breaks = paste0("item.", 1:12), labels = names(quiz)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = NULL, x = "Political knowledge (θ)", y = "Information", color = NULL)

(Here the items are called “item.1” to “item.12”, with a dot. Small inconsistencies like this are common in packages; printing unique(p$data$key) for a plot p shows what the data call them.)

Then the test information, the sum of the curves above. testInfoPlot() also draws the standard error, \(1 / \sqrt{I(\theta)}\), on the right-hand axis; adj_factor sets how that axis is scaled.

ggmirt::testInfoPlot(irt_fixed_g, adj_factor = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(information = "#2f1a61", SE = "#cc0065")) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = NULL, x = "Political knowledge (θ)", color = NULL, linetype = NULL)

Information is high, and the standard error low, in the middle of the scale. At both ends, few items are informative, and the standard error grows.

Activity 💡

You may only use five of the twelve items. Two clients want a short form:

  • a civic education NGO that wants to identify people with very low knowledge (\(\theta\) around −1.5), to target a program, and
  • a selection committee that wants to rank the most knowledgeable applicants (\(\theta\) around +1.5).
  1. For each client, pick the five items with the most information at their target \(\theta\). (Hint: filter icc to the \(\theta\) closest to the target, then dplyr::slice_max(info, n = 5).)
  2. Plot the test information of both short forms over the whole range of \(\theta\). Where is each one precise, and where is it nearly blind?
➨ Click for Answer 🔓 
best_five <- function(target) {
  icc %>%
    dplyr::filter(abs(theta - target) < 0.001) %>%
    dplyr::slice_max(info, n = 5) %>%
    dplyr::pull(item)
}

short_forms <- list("NGO (θ = -1.5)" = best_five(-1.5),
                    "Selection (θ = +1.5)" = best_five(1.5))
short_forms
$`NGO (θ = -1.5)`
[1] "q03" "q01" "q02" "q04" "q05"

$`Selection (θ = +1.5)`
[1] "q11" "q09" "q10" "q08" "q12"
purrr::map(short_forms, \(chosen) {
  icc %>%
    dplyr::filter(item %in% chosen) %>%
    dplyr::group_by(theta) %>%
    dplyr::summarize(info = sum(info))
}) %>%
  purrr::list_rbind(names_to = "short_form") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = theta, y = info, color = short_form)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#2f1a61", "#cc0065")) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Political knowledge (θ)", y = "Test information", color = "Short form")
  1. The NGO’s form is made of the easy items, the selection form of the hard ones, and both favor highly discriminating items.
  2. Each short form is precise around its target and nearly blind at the other end: the NGO’s form cannot tell a knowledgeable person from a very knowledgeable one, and the selection form cannot tell apart people who know little from people who know nothing. Neither is a bad test; they answer different questions. Notice also that the NGO’s form peaks around θ ≈ −0.8, not at its target of −1.5. With guessing, each item’s information peaks a little above its difficulty: at the very low end, many correct answers are lucky guesses and carry little evidence. Multiple-choice items struggle to measure precisely at the bottom of the scale. This is the INSPIRE logic from the seminar: decide where the measure must be precise (for us, at the low end, where policy acts) before choosing items.

Bonus: IRT for the trust battery (graded response model) 🪜

IRT is not only for right/wrong answers. The graded response model (GRM) handles ordered categories: each item has one discrimination and a set of thresholds between adjacent categories. Eleven categories (0–10) are more than the data can support for thresholds, so we group them into five, as in the seminar’s auxiliary slides, using cut() from Lab 4:

trust_grouped <- trust %>%
  dplyr::select(parliament:dont_care_r) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(everything(), \(x) {
    as.integer(cut(x, breaks = c(-Inf, 2, 4, 5, 7, Inf))) # 0-2, 3-4, 5, 6-7, 8-10
  }))

irt_grm <- mirt::mirt(trust_grouped, 1, itemtype = "graded", verbose = FALSE)

coef(irt_grm, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items %>%
  round(2)
               a    b1    b2   b3   b4
parliament  2.86 -1.49 -0.31 0.28 1.42
politicians 2.07 -1.76 -0.34 0.36 1.69
parties     2.04 -1.67 -0.32 0.32 1.61
government  1.93 -1.72 -0.36 0.37 1.67
dont_care_r 0.99 -2.71 -0.48 0.45 2.60

a is the discrimination; b1 to b4 are the points on the latent scale where answering above each category becomes more likely than not. The reverse-coded item discriminates least, as its loading in the CFA did.

With facet = TRUE, tracePlot() draws one panel per item. For a GRM, each panel shows the probability of each answer category along the latent scale:

ggmirt::tracePlot(irt_grm, facet = TRUE, legend = TRUE) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(labels = c("0-2", "3-4", "5", "6-7", "8-10"), end = 0.9) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = NULL, x = "Representative trust (θ)", y = "P(category)", color = "Answer")
ggmirt::testInfoPlot(irt_grm, adj_factor = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(information = "#2f1a61", SE = "#cc0065")) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = NULL, x = "Representative trust (θ)", color = NULL, linetype = NULL)

With many ordered categories, the thresholds are spread out, so the battery is informative over a wide range of trust, unlike a short quiz of right/wrong items.

Part IV (optional): Does the measure travel? 🌍

⚠️ This part is optional, for you to work through on your own if you are interested. Martín will not cover it in the lab. It follows, to some extent, the approach that Davidov et al. (2014, Annual Review of Sociology) lay out: test configural, metric, and scalar invariance with a multigroup CFA, and consider partial invariance when full invariance fails.

Three countries 🗺

We now survey three countries with the same eight items. They differ in their latent means, and in Country C something else is going on: people answer the police item about 1.2 points more positively than their order trust would predict. (Think of a country where saying you distrust the police is socially risky, or where “the police” means a different institution.) That is a violation of scalar invariance in one item.

First, a small wrapper around make_trust() that adds a country label. The ... passes any other arguments (the latent means, the police shift) straight on to make_trust():

make_country <- function(country, n, ...) {
  tibble::tibble(country = country, make_trust(n, ...))
}

We store the country parameters in a table and use purrr::pmap() again, this time to call make_country() once per row. pmap() matches the columns to the arguments by name, and ... collects the ones make_country() does not name itself:

countries <- tibble::tibble(
  country = c("Country A", "Country B", "Country C"),
  n = 800,
  mean_rep = c(0, -0.4, 0.2), # latent mean of representative trust
  mean_ord = c(0, 0.1, -0.2), # latent mean of order trust
  police_shift = c(0, 0, 0.6) # Country C answers the police item more positively
)

trust_3 <- purrr::pmap(countries, make_country) %>%
  purrr::list_rbind()

dplyr::count(trust_3, country)

n = 800 is recycled to every row, so each country has 800 respondents. police_shift = 0.6 is on the scale of the raw item, which make_trust() multiplies by 2, hence ≈ 1.2 points on the 0–10 scale.

First, the naive comparison: the average of the three order items, by country.

trust_3 %>%
  dplyr::mutate(order_scale = rowMeans(dplyr::across(c(courts, police, civil_service)))) %>%
  dplyr::group_by(country) %>%
  dplyr::summarize(dplyr::across(c(courts, police, civil_service, order_scale), mean)) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2)))

On the averaged scale, Country C looks like it trusts order institutions at least as much as Country A. We know that in truth it trusts them less (latent mean −0.2). The police item carries the whole difference.

Configural, metric, scalar ⛓

From the seminar, each level of invariance adds equality constraints to a multigroup CFA:

  • configural: the same items load on the same factors in every country;
  • metric: plus equal loadings (group.equal = "loadings");
  • scalar: plus equal intercepts (group.equal = c("loadings", "intercepts")).

We fit all three with purrr::map() over a list of constraints, then reuse fit_table() from Part II:

constraints <- list(
  configural = character(0), # no equality constraints
  metric = "loadings",
  scalar = c("loadings", "intercepts")
)

invariance_fits <- purrr::map(constraints, \(eq) {
  lavaan::cfa(model_two, data = trust_3, group = "country", group.equal = eq)
})

invariance_fits %>%
  purrr::map(fit_table) %>%
  purrr::list_rbind(names_to = "level")
lavaan::lavTestLRT(invariance_fits$configural, invariance_fits$metric, invariance_fits$scalar)

Constraining the loadings costs nothing: metric invariance holds. Constraining the intercepts makes fit much worse (a large χ² difference, and CFI falls by far more than the usual 0.01 threshold): scalar invariance fails. The structure travels; the scale does not.

Finding the culprit 🔎

Under metric invariance, the intercepts are free in each country, and the latent means are fixed at zero. So each intercept absorbs that country’s latent mean, multiplied by the item’s loading: \(\nu_{jg} = \nu_j + \lambda_j \kappa_g\). Dividing the intercept difference by the loading gives the latent mean difference implied by each item. If an item is invariant, all items of a factor should imply roughly the same difference:

group_labels <- lavaan::lavInspect(invariance_fits$metric, "group.label")

est_metric <- lavaan::parameterEstimates(invariance_fits$metric) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(country = group_labels[group])

loadings_metric <- est_metric %>%
  dplyr::filter(op == "=~", country == "Country A") %>%
  dplyr::select(factor = lhs, item = rhs, loading = est)

est_metric %>%
  dplyr::filter(op == "~1", lhs %in% names(items)) %>%
  dplyr::select(item = lhs, country, intercept = est) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = country, values_from = intercept) %>%
  dplyr::left_join(loadings_metric, by = "item") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(`B vs A` = (`Country B` - `Country A`) / loading,
                `C vs A` = (`Country C` - `Country A`) / loading) %>%
  dplyr::select(factor, item, `B vs A`, `C vs A`) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2)))

Within each factor, the items agree, except one: police implies that Country C trusts order institutions far more than A, while courts and civil_service imply that it trusts them less. (The implied differences are in units of each factor’s marker item, parliament and courts, which lavaan used to set the scale.)

Partial scalar invariance 🩹

Davidov et al. (2014) discuss what researchers can do when full scalar invariance fails. One option is partial invariance: free the intercept of the offending item, keep the rest equal, and compare latent means using the invariant items. In lavaan, group.partial lists the parameters to release from the constraints; "police ~ 1" is the intercept of police:

partial_scalar <- lavaan::cfa(model_two, data = trust_3, group = "country",
                              group.equal = c("loadings", "intercepts"),
                              group.partial = "police ~ 1")

fit_table(partial_scalar)
lavaan::lavTestLRT(invariance_fits$metric, partial_scalar)

Freeing one intercept restores the fit: the partial scalar model is no worse than the metric model.

Activity 💡

In a scalar model, lavaan fixes the latent means to zero in the first country and estimates them in the others (op == "~1" and lhs a factor in parameterEstimates()).

  1. Extract the latent means of representative and order in Countries B and C, from both the full scalar model and the partial scalar model. To compare them with the truth, divide each one by the latent standard deviation in Country A (op == "~~" with lhs == rhs a factor, group == 1, then sqrt()).
  2. Which model gets the order mean of Country C right? Which one pulls it toward zero? What about the representative means?
  3. Rerun the whole analysis with police_shift = 0 for Country C. Does scalar invariance hold now?
➨ Click for Answer 🔓 
latent_means <- function(fit) {
  est <- lavaan::parameterEstimates(fit) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(country = group_labels[group])

  sd_a <- est %>%
    dplyr::filter(op == "~~", lhs == rhs, lhs %in% c("representative", "order"),
                  country == "Country A") %>%
    dplyr::transmute(factor = lhs, sd_a = sqrt(est))

  est %>%
    dplyr::filter(op == "~1", lhs %in% c("representative", "order"),
                  country != "Country A") %>%
    dplyr::select(factor = lhs, country, mean = est) %>%
    dplyr::left_join(sd_a, by = "factor") %>%
    dplyr::transmute(factor, country, mean_in_sd = round(mean / sd_a, 2))
}

truth <- countries %>%
  dplyr::filter(country != "Country A") %>%
  dplyr::select(country, representative = mean_rep, order = mean_ord) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-country, names_to = "factor", values_to = "truth")

list("Full scalar" = invariance_fits$scalar, "Partial scalar" = partial_scalar) %>%
  purrr::map(latent_means) %>%
  purrr::list_rbind(names_to = "model") %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = model, values_from = mean_in_sd) %>%
  dplyr::left_join(truth, by = c("factor", "country")) %>%
  dplyr::arrange(factor, country)
# 3. no police shift in Country C
trust_3_invariant <- countries %>%
  dplyr::mutate(police_shift = 0) %>%
  purrr::pmap(make_country) %>%
  purrr::list_rbind()

purrr::map(constraints, \(eq) {
  lavaan::cfa(model_two, data = trust_3_invariant, group = "country", group.equal = eq)
}) %>%
  purrr::map(fit_table) %>%
  purrr::list_rbind(names_to = "level")
  1. The partial scalar model recovers all four latent means, up to sampling noise.
  2. The full scalar model forces the police intercept to be equal, so the extra positivity of Country C’s police answers is read as more order trust: the order mean for C is pulled toward zero, and most of the true gap with Country A disappears. With a larger shift, it would change sign. The representative means are almost unaffected, because the non-invariant item belongs to the other factor.
  3. Without the police shift, the scalar model fits about as well as the metric model: the scale now travels, and comparing means across the three countries is justified.

⚠️ In our simulation we knew which item was non-invariant. In real data you look for it with the evidence above (or with lavaan::lavTestScore()), and you should have a substantive reason for freeing an item, ideally stated before you see the results. Freeing intercepts until the model fits is another fork in the path. And partial invariance needs at least two invariant items per factor to identify the latent means.

Wrap-up 🎁

  • EFA lets the data suggest a structure: decide the number of factors with parallel analysis (not eigenvalues > 1), use an oblique rotation, and name the factors yourself.
  • CFA tests a structure you write down. Compare competing theories with fit indices and a likelihood-ratio test, and use residual correlations to see where a model fails.
  • McDonald’s ω uses the fitted loadings and is computed per factor; it is only as good as the model behind it.
  • IRT models the probability of each answer. Model comparison picks what the data can support, and knowledge of the test’s design (four options, so a guessing floor of 0.25) can do what the data cannot. Information curves show where a test is precise, which is a design choice.
  • Optional Part IV: measurement invariance. Metric invariance lets you compare relationships across groups; comparing means needs (at least partial) scalar invariance. A single non-invariant item can reverse a cross-country comparison.
  • R skills from today: matrix algebra for simulation (%*%), purrr::reduce(), purrr::pmap() over the rows of a parameter table, tidyr::expand_grid(), tidying model output into tibbles for plots, ready-made plots from {ggmirt} restyled with ggplot2 syntax, and model syntax in {lavaan}.
